name: Common Buckwheat
summary: A fast-growing annual used as a short-window cover crop. University of Minnesota Extension reports quick establishment, weed suppression and flowers that support beneficial insects; its regional planting windows should not be generalized to every climate.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Fagopyrum esculentum. This profile represents common buckwheat, not a named grain or cover-crop variety.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes buckwheat as quick to establish and useful for weed suppression. Its crop-selection guidance is regional and does not establish indoor or hydroponic performance.

cultivation.short: Useful in a warm-season cover-crop window
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension lists June 10–August 15 as a Minnesota planting window and gives field seeding-rate guidance. Treat these as regional cover-crop references, not a local calendar or container rate.

management.short: Allow bloom, then terminate before seed set
management.guidance: UMN Extension reports that buckwheat flowers attract pollinators and natural enemies, but the crop also goes to seed quickly. For cover-crop use, plan termination around flowering before seed set to reduce volunteer plants. UMN describes a roughly 45–50-day cover-crop window in its regional rotation guidance; this is not a cultivar-specific maturity date or a guarantee for every garden.

propagation.short: Sowing is documented; home seedling protocol incomplete
propagation.guidance: Extension sources document planting windows and field seeding rates, but do not establish a complete home-garden sowing depth, germination temperature or seedling-stage protocol. Those details remain unresolved.

problems.short: Rapid seed set can create volunteer buckwheat
problems.guidance: UMN Extension warns that buckwheat can go to seed quickly and should be mowed or terminated at flowering to prevent reseeding. This is a cover-crop management risk, not a disease diagnosis or a claim about a named variety.

name: Crimson Clover
summary: An annual legume cover crop used for nitrogen contribution and soil cover. University of Minnesota guidance describes regional use and cautions that a pure stand may become weedy; it is not a hydroponic crop profile.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Trifolium incarnatum in Fabaceae. No named cultivar or seed product is represented.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes crimson clover as a legume used in cover-crop mixes and identifies its nitrogen contribution. The evidence is for agricultural/vegetable cover-crop use in Minnesota.

cultivation.short: Planting dates and rate depend on region and mix
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension recommends planting clover before grasses in a mix so the grass does not overtake it. Its planting recommendations and field rates are Minnesota references, not a universal garden schedule.

management.short: Use in a planned mix; clover should establish before grasses
management.guidance: UMN Extension describes crimson clover as a nitrogen-fixing cover-crop legume that can contribute some weed suppression in mixtures. It recommends sowing clover before grasses so the grass does not overtake it; flowers may support beneficial insects if the stand is allowed to bloom. These are Minnesota cover-crop observations, not a home-garden yield guarantee.

propagation.short: Seeded cover crop; detailed home protocol unresolved
propagation.guidance: The selected sources establish seeding as the cover-crop route and provide regional planting context, but do not document a complete home seed-starting protocol, depth or germination conditions.

problems.short: A pure stand may become weedy
problems.guidance: UMN Extension cautions that crimson clover may become weedy when grown alone. Consider the crop's role in a planned cover-crop mix and local termination needs; the source does not define a universal home-garden control schedule.

name: White Clover
summary: A perennial legume used in groundcover and cover-crop mixes. Extension guidance supports nitrogen contribution and soil-cover functions; this species-level record does not claim a lawn cultivar or edible use.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Trifolium repens. This record is the species and not a named lawn or microclover selection.

growth.short: Low perennial mats spread by creeping, rooting stems
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes white clover as a low-growing perennial forming mats about 3–12 inches tall and 1–2 feet across. Smooth creeping stems root at nodes; rounded three-part leaves often show a pale crescent, and small white-to-pink flower clusters commonly bloom from spring into early fall. These are Minnesota landscape observations, not dimensions for a named lawn cultivar.

cultivation.short: Cool, moist soil and partial sun suit this groundcover
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension reports that white clover thrives in cool, moist soil with partial sun and does poorly in shade and heavy foot traffic. This describes outdoor landscape conditions; it does not establish an indoor grow-light tier or hydroponic suitability.

management.short: Useful as groundcover, living mulch, or a pollinator planting
management.guidance: UMN Extension describes white clover use in bee lawns, pastures, cover crops, green manures, and living mulches. Because it spreads by stolons, it may persist outside a short cover-crop window; UMN advises digging or hand-pulling small unwanted patches. No named turf cultivar or universal termination method is represented.

propagation.short: Seeded cover crop; establishment details need validation
propagation.guidance: The Extension cover-crop guide supports use of white clover as a seeded cover crop but does not provide a complete home-garden germination protocol in the selected material. Depth and seedling-care details remain unresolved.

problems.short: Persistent mats may spread where they are not wanted
problems.guidance: UMN Extension notes that white clover can be undesirable in some lawns, spreads through creeping stems that root at nodes, and may be associated with low soil nitrogen, compaction, or drought stress. Treat those associations as clues to inspect site conditions, not as a diagnosis from clover presence alone.

name: Cereal Rye
summary: A cool-season cereal widely used as an overwintering cover crop. University of Minnesota Extension describes reliable establishment and spring growth in Minnesota; management must account for termination before the next crop.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Secale cereale as a cultivated cereal species. This entry represents cereal rye, not annual ryegrass (Lolium) or a named grain cultivar.

growth.short: Cool-season cereal used for winter soil cover
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes cereal rye as a common Minnesota cover crop that germinates at cool temperatures, establishes reliably and overwinters in the region. Performance depends on climate and planting window.

cultivation.short: Field timing is regional and rotation-dependent
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension lists regional planting windows and field-scale seeding rates. Its Minnesota dates should not be copied as a universal home-garden calendar or a container sowing rate.

management.short: Plan spring termination before the next crop
management.guidance: UMN Extension describes vigorous spring growth and recommends planning termination before the following crop. In its field guidance, mowing or roller-crimping is most reliable at flowering or heading; allow roughly three weeks for residue breakdown before planting where that rotation guidance applies. These are regional field methods, not a universal small-garden schedule.

propagation.guidance: UMN sources document drilling and field establishment, but do not establish a complete small-garden seedling protocol for this identity. Field rates and row geometry should not be presented as indoor pod guidance.

problems.short: Mature rye can be difficult to terminate and leave a dense residue
problems.guidance: UMN Extension notes that winter rye can be hard to kill and may form a thick mat. Later, more mature residue decomposes more slowly and can compete for nitrogen with the next crop; the timing and effect depend on the field system and termination stage.

name: Oats
summary: A cool-season annual cereal profile focused on oats as a short-window cover and nurse crop in Minnesota vegetable-garden guidance. The entry covers rapid establishment, soil-cover functions, winter-kill and residue management; it does not represent a grain or forage cultivar.

identity.short: Accepted cultivated cereal species; cover-crop use represented
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Avena sativa. This Gardenpedia entry represents the species in its cover-crop category; no grain cultivar, forage selection or seed product is specified.

growth.short: Annual cool-season crop; quick establishment in cover-crop use
growth.guidance: Kew identifies Avena sativa as an annual cultivated species. UMN Extension describes oats as quick to establish in vegetable-garden cover-crop use. In Minnesota, this annual does not survive winter; that regional winter-kill behavior can be useful when a cover is wanted without a living spring stand.

cultivation.short: Fast cover, nitrogen scavenging and residue that breaks down quickly
cultivation.guidance: For Minnesota vegetable growers, UMN Extension describes oats as readily available and affordable, with nitrogen scavenging, erosion prevention and weed-control benefits. The page cautions that these functions may be somewhat weaker than overwintering cereals, while the residue breaks down quickly enough to allow earlier spring planting. It also documents mixing oats with peas or berseem clover. These are cover-crop functions in a regional field/garden context, not a grain-yield claim, container rate or universal performance promise.

management.short: Choose the termination window for the cover-crop role
management.guidance: UMN Extension says oats used as an early-spring cover can be terminated at any point; unlike spring barley or wheat in the same guide, mechanical termination does not require waiting until flowering. Oats also serve as a nurse crop that keeps weed pressure lower while clover establishes. Because oats die over winter in Minnesota, UMN notes that they may not suit permanent beds needing a living perennial cover; a perennial grass such as fescue may fit that role better. These are system-specific management distinctions, not pesticide guidance.

propagation.short: Seed-sown cover; exact home-scale protocol not established here
propagation.guidance: UMN documents oats as a seeded cover crop and nurse crop in vegetable rotations. Its regional selection page does not establish a universal home sowing depth, indoor germination protocol or container rate; field rates should not be converted to hydroponic pod spacing.

problems.short: Winter-kill is useful in some rotations but a limitation in permanent cover
problems.guidance: UMN Extension states that oats are annual and will not survive the Minnesota winter. This is an expected lifecycle trait, not a disease: it can simplify termination when winter-kill is desired, but leaves no living oat cover in spring. The source does not establish a universal cold threshold outside its regional context.

name: Alpine Strawberry
summary: A day-neutral species with small, sweet fruit. UMN distinguishes woodland/alpine strawberry from a named garden-strawberry cultivar, but its guide both describes runner variation among seed-grown Fragaria vesca and lists the alpine type as runner-free; this unspecified species record does not assume one behavior.

identity.short: Accepted species, distinct from garden strawberry cultivars
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Fragaria vesca. UMN Extension identifies alpine/woodland strawberry as a distinct species/type, not a named cultivar of Monterey strawberry; the entry does not assign a selection.

growth.short: Usually compact; runner production can vary in seed-grown plants
growth.guidance: UMN describes Fragaria vesca as a day-neutral woodland/alpine strawberry with small, sweet fruit. The same guide says seed-grown woodland strawberries may or may not produce runners, while its alpine-type table describes alpine plants as runner-free. Because no seed selection is represented here, runner production is treated as variable rather than a universal species trait.

cultivation.short: Suitable for beds, walkways or containers in its regional guide
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension says woodland strawberries tolerate shadier sites and can be planted in perennial beds, walkways or containers. Its general Minnesota strawberry guidance recommends regular moisture (about 1 inch of rainfall per week); this is a soil-garden reference, not a fixed container or hydroponic schedule.

harvest.short: Small, sweet berries; yield differs from large-fruited types
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes small, sweet fruit and gives an approximate species-type yield of two to three berries per plant per week. This should not be generalized to other strawberry species or cultivars.

propagation.short: Seed-grown plants are represented; germination protocol not established
propagation.guidance: UMN notes that alpine strawberry plants are commonly grown from seed, but the selected source does not supply a complete sowing depth, temperature or germination protocol. Keep those details unresolved.

maintenance.short: Check for runners and manage only when present
maintenance.guidance: UMN says seed-grown Fragaria vesca may or may not produce runners, while its general strawberry guidance recommends removing unwanted runners to control spread. For this unspecified seed-grown selection, inspect the established plant and remove runners only if they appear and expansion is not desired.

problems.short: Wet fruit and poor airflow can favor strawberry diseases
problems.guidance: UMN describes fruit rots and leaf diseases across strawberries and advises practices that help foliage and fruit dry. Treat this as crop-group prevention, not evidence of a Fragaria vesca-specific disease or resistance: watch for soft/decaying fruit, remove affected berries, and avoid prolonged surface wetness where practical.

growthHabits.reason: UMN's page gives both a runner-free alpine-type description and a caveat that seed-grown Fragaria vesca may or may not produce runners; no specific seed selection is represented.

name: Black Chokeberry
summary: A hardy deciduous shrub with edible but strongly astringent fruit, usually processed rather than eaten fresh. The species has landscape, wildlife and fruit uses; no named cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Aronia melanocarpa and records the common name black chokeberry. This is not chokecherry (Prunus virginiana), and no cultivar such as ‘Viking’ or ‘Autumn Magic’ is assigned.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes a deciduous shrub about 3–8 ft tall and 2–6 ft wide in its Minnesota landscape profile. It can sucker and form dense plantings; those regional dimensions are not a container-size promise.

cultivation.guidance: UMN reports full sun, tolerance of partial shade and broad soil/moisture tolerance, including wet soils, in Minnesota. These landscape conditions do not establish indoor or hydroponic suitability.

harvest.guidance: UMN describes dark fruit used in jams, juice, wine and baking, and notes it is too astringent for most people to eat raw. The source does not establish a home harvest calendar for an unnamed selection.

problems.short: Suckering and browsing are useful management signals
problems.guidance: UMN reports stronger suckering in cultivated landscapes and browsing by deer and rabbits; it lists no serious pest or stress problem in its regional profile. Absence from that list is not a guarantee of pest-free growth.

propagation.short: Aronia is propagated by seed or cuttings in fruit-crop production
propagation.guidance: University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension reports that Aronia is commonly propagated by seed or cuttings. This is fruit-crop production guidance, not a complete household protocol; no seed-starting or cutting schedule is inferred here.

flowering.short: White spring flowers, autumn color and fruit that may persist
flowering.guidance: UMN describes showy white flower clusters about 2–3 inches across with pink anthers in spring. The deciduous foliage changes from green to red, orange and purple in autumn; dark fruit may persist into winter and feed wildlife. These are seasonal cues from UMN's Minnesota species profile, not fixed dates or traits assigned to an unnamed cultivar.

name: Honeyberry
summary: A cold-hardy blue-fruited honeysuckle crop also called haskap. Reliable fruiting requires a different, compatible variety blooming at the same time; this species record does not name a cultivar or imply a universal pollinizer pair.

metrics.label: Reported shrub size
metrics.value: About 1.2–2 m tall; roughly 1.2–1.8 m wide
metrics.note: Extension descriptions vary with variety and region; not a named-cultivar guarantee

metrics.label: Home-garden spacing
metrics.note: USask guidance; outdoor soil spacing, not pod spacing

identity.short: Accepted species; cultivar and subspecies unspecified
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lonicera caerulea. Honeyberry and haskap are names for the cultivated edible-blue-honeysuckle crop, but this profile does not assign a subspecies or named cultivar.

growth.short: Cold-hardy shrub; form and size vary by variety
growth.guidance: USask describes a rounded home-garden shrub about 1.2–2 m tall and around 1.2 m wide. USU notes that forms vary from low-growing to upright and may reach about 1.8 m in height and spread. Treat these as regional, variety-dependent descriptions rather than the dimensions of an unspecified cultivar; the shrub has a broad, shallow root system.

cultivation.short: Full sun and compatible, overlapping bloom for fruit
cultivation.guidance: For home gardens, USask recommends full sun for best fruiting; part sun can produce less fruit. Haskap tolerates several soil types but does best in well-drained loam or sandy loam; clay is suitable only where drainage is good. Keep a newly planted shrub moist, not waterlogged, for its first 2–3 weeks. Allow at least 1 m between outdoor shrubs, as USask advises; this is garden spacing, not indoor pod spacing. Haskap is self-incompatible: plant a different compatible variety whose bloom overlaps. No pollinizer pair can be named for this unspecified cultivar, so confirm compatibility with the nursery or cultivar chart before buying.

harvest.short: Harvest dark-blue fruit when ripe; timing is regional and variety-dependent
harvest.guidance: USask reports a late-June to early-July harvest window for Saskatchewan, not a universal calendar. UMN describes a short, variety-dependent window and recommends tasting for ripeness; color alone can be misleading. For fresh-market use, the Minnesota U-Pick guidance favors hand-picking to preserve fruit integrity; mechanical shaking is discussed for frozen or wholesale channels, not as a universal home method.

problems.short: Watch for birds, powdery mildew and warm-site stress
problems.guidance: UMN notes birds and powdery mildew as possible crop problems. USU reports that warmer sites can bring scorching, mildew and premature leaf drop, with susceptibility differing among Russian and Japanese types; this identity does not assign a subspecies, so treat these as regional risks rather than guaranteed symptoms. USU notes pruning for airflow can help limit mildew; no cultivar-specific resistance is implied.

propagation.short: Nursery transplants and cuttings are common production routes
propagation.guidance: Ontario’s specialty-crop guidance lists tissue-culture transplants and softwood or hardwood cuttings as common propagation methods for haskap. This establishes crop-level vegetative routes, not a step-by-step home protocol or a seed-germination method; seek a nursery-grown, correctly labeled cultivar when cultivar identity and compatible pollination matter.

management.short: Light dormant pruning can protect access to fruiting branches
management.guidance: UMN Extension describes dormant pruning to prevent low branches from drooping under fruit weight; opening the canopy for access and aeration is presented specifically for U-Pick operations. USU also notes that pruning for airflow can help with powdery mildew. No cultivar-specific pruning calendar or hard annual pruning rule is established here.

growthHabits.reason: The existing compatibility vocabulary does not encode shrub growth form.

spread.reason: Reported shrub widths vary by variety and region; indoor footprint is not established.

spacing.reason: Orchard and home-garden spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light intensity tier.

name: Lingonberry
summary: Low evergreen berry subshrub grown in acidic, well-drained conditions. Cultivar identity affects growth and crop timing; the general species entry avoids assigning Pacific Northwest cultivar dimensions or a fixed harvest calendar.

identity.short: Accepted species; common name cowberry is also used
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Vaccinium vitis-idaea and records cowberry among its English common names. The identity is not American cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon), already represented separately.

growth.guidance: Kew describes the accepted species as a subshrub. UMN Extension includes lingonberry as a low-growing edible landscape plant in its Minnesota comparison table; no specific cultivar is assigned.

cultivation.short: Acidic soil, steady moisture, and good drainage
cultivation.guidance: Oregon State's Pacific Northwest production guide gives soil pH 4.3–5.5, favors light, well-drained soil, and warns that lingonberry is sensitive to sodium and chloride salts. Keep the root zone from drying completely while avoiding saturation and root-rot conditions. These are crop-production values from the Pacific Northwest, not hydroponic solution targets.

harvest.short: Harvest berries when red, not while still green
harvest.guidance: Oregon State says berries range from light to dark red at harvest and can taste bitter when picked green. It describes summer and fall crops and cultivar-dependent timing; no single season, color threshold, or storage duration is assigned to this unnamed entry.

propagation.short: Cuttings preserve a clone; seedlings may differ from the parent
propagation.guidance: Oregon State describes micropropagation and stem cuttings as common production methods and notes that seedling plants may not be true to parent stock. It also reports limitations of cuttings and divisions in commercial fields. No named cultivar is assigned here, and seed-to-seedling establishment remains in the Seed Profile.

pollination.short: Compatible flowering cultivars support berry size and crop
pollination.guidance: Oregon State reports that lingonberry production benefits from pollinizer cultivars and pollinating insects. Its field ratio and named pollinizers are commercial Pacific Northwest recommendations; this unnamed species profile does not assign a cultivar pair or a home-garden planting ratio.

maintenance.short: Do not prune young field plantings by default
maintenance.guidance: Oregon State reports no pruning recommendation for the first four to five years after field planting and says the best later pruning method is not established; it describes alternate-row mowing only in its commercial system. Avoid turning that field treatment into a routine home-pruning instruction.

problems.short: Watch for berry loss, root rot, and locally reported leaf or twig disease
problems.guidance: The Pacific Northwest guide reports bird damage to ripening berries and several fungal diseases in regional plantings; it also links waterlogged conditions with root-rot risk. Use these as scouting cues, not a claim that every plant is affected or that a symptom alone diagnoses a pathogen. The guide recommends laboratory diagnosis where disease identity matters.

name: Saskatoon Serviceberry
summary: The deciduous Saskatoon serviceberry is a North American shrub or small tree grown for sweet blue-purple berries and ornamental value. Species-specific size varies widely; full sun and drained soil support fruiting, while uneven ripening calls for repeated harvests.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Amelanchier alnifolia. NC State Extension names Saskatoon serviceberry and Juneberry for this species; the broader common name ‘serviceberry’ can refer to several Amelanchier species. No cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Deciduous, upright shrub or small tree; adult size varies widely
growth.guidance: NC State describes this species as an erect deciduous shrub, commonly listed at 3–18 ft tall; its structured table gives 6–10 ft width, while the page narrative says 6–8 ft and notes exceptional height up to 30 ft in rich, moist soil. These are broad landscape ranges, not a named cultivar's dimensions. Utah State Extension also cautions that serviceberry size depends on species and cultivar.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil favor fruit; keep establishment moist, not waterlogged
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and rich, well-drained loam for best berries and long-lasting flowers, while noting tolerance across a range of light and moisture conditions. Utah State Extension's genus-level home-garden guide advises keeping the first-season root zone moist but not wet; clay soil and poor drainage can promote root problems. It recommends watering at the base and mulching to retain moisture. The Utah schedule is regional; no cultivar-specific irrigation amount or hydroponic recipe is implied.

harvest.short: Blue-purple fruit ripens unevenly; pick in several passes and cool promptly
harvest.guidance: NC State describes sweet, edible blue-purple fruit ripening in early summer. The University of Saskatchewan reports uneven ripening and repeated picking for Saskatoon; its prairie dates are not universal. Utah State Extension's broader serviceberry guide recommends harvesting when about two-thirds of the fruit is ripe, by hand while fruit is dry and cool, then sorting, washing and drying it before refrigeration or freezing. Prompt cooling matters because USask reports rapid quality decline after harvest.

propagation.short: Seed, suckers and cuttings are documented; seed-grown plants may not stay true to type
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed, sucker separation, spring hardwood cuttings and summer softwood cuttings for A. alnifolia. Utah State Extension describes transplanting suckers from a healthy established serviceberry before bud break as a practical vegetative route; it cautions that seedlings may not reproduce the parent and that hardwood/softwood cutting success is limited. These are species/genus-level options, not a cultivar-preserving guarantee for an unidentified plant.

care.short: Maintain moisture for fruit quality and avoid wetting the canopy
care.guidance: Utah State Extension says established serviceberries can survive with little water, but irrigation supports maximum yield and desirable fruit; extra water may be needed in hot, dry weather. Watering at the shrub base helps keep foliage dry, and mulch helps conserve soil moisture. Its quantitative schedule is Utah guidance, not a universal requirement for every site or cultivar.

pruning.short: Prune before spring growth and retain fruiting-age wood
pruning.guidance: Utah State Extension's genus-level guide recommends pruning in late winter or early spring before new growth. It notes that serviceberry flowers form on 2–4-year-old stems; removing about one-third of older growth annually is offered as a way to maintain younger fruiting wood and an open canopy. Apply this as general serviceberry guidance, not a cultivar-specific pruning prescription.

flowering.short: Fragrant white clusters appear in spring, often before leaves
flowering.guidance: NC State describes compact clusters of fragrant white flowers appearing in spring before the shrub's leaves. The same source notes summer fruit and yellow-to-red fall foliage, giving the species ornamental interest beyond flowering. No fixed local bloom date is assigned.

problems.short: Protect ripening fruit from birds and monitor leaf spots and rust
problems.guidance: Utah State Extension reports birds as a major fruit-loss risk; its guide also describes angular brown Entomosporium leaf spots with yellow rings, gray spots on affected fruit, white powdery mildew and Saskatoon-juniper rust. Rust may begin as yellow spots/swelling and develop yellow spiky growths; the guide advises avoiding nearby junipers where this disease is a concern. NC State lists additional pests and diseases for the species. These are monitoring cues, not proof of diagnosis or a claim that every plant is affected; no pesticide prescription is made.

uses.short: Edible berries and a multi-season ornamental shrub
uses.guidance: NC State and Minnesota Extension describe the fruit as edible and useful fresh or in preserves. Fragrant spring flowers, summer berries and fall foliage also support ornamental and wildlife value. Food preparation details are handled separately in Harvest Use; this profile does not imply medicinal benefits.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility vocabulary does not represent shrub/tree form without ambiguity.

height.reason: NC State reports 3–18 ft in its structured dimensions and up to 30 ft in rich, moist soil; no single compatibility maximum is selected for this broad species record.

spread.reason: NC State's narrative gives 6–8 ft while its structured table gives 6–10 ft; the disagreement is retained rather than presented as a precise system footprint.

spacing.reason: Landscape dimensions do not establish a universal planting distance or pod spacing.

evidence.note: NC State recommends full outdoor sun for best berries and long-lasting flowers; its broader shade tolerance is not an indoor grow-light tier.
